assumptions: That the 23:59 deploy is related to the incident at all: this rests entirely on the one-minute gap between the deploy and the first latency warning. Nothing in the logs ties the slowdown to the new revision, and the hypothesis was never tested by rollback or any other means.

That the deploy was the only change in play. The change-event source returned exactly one record for every window queried, from 24 hours to roughly six weeks; that infrastructure, configuration, downstream-service and datastore changes not carried by that source did not occur is assumed, not verified.

That the absence of recent feature-flag changes rules flags out. The flag provider's history was read and showed nothing recent, which is the one negative result the investigation actually established.

The investigation placed the start of the incident at 00:01 from a four-minute metrics window anchored on 00:02. That window is short and begins after the deploy, so the pre-incident baseline is taken from the log line citing a 220ms baseline rather than from observed pre-deploy metrics.

That the incident is over. The recorded end time coincides exactly with the escalation to a human, and no recovery was observed, confirmed, or caused by any action described here. The service may have self-recovered, the load may have subsided, or the condition may have persisted past the point the automation stopped watching.

The three investigation passes read overlapping copies of the same six log lines and reached the same conclusion each time; they are treated as one body of evidence, not three independent confirmations.
input.executive_summary: Shortly after midnight UTC on 14 September, one service began responding slowly and then timing out; a share of requests that would normally have succeeded failed instead, for a period of a few minutes. Automated response picked the incident up within the same second the alert fired, and the automation cycled three times through the same investigation: it read the service's recent metrics and logs, searched for recent production changes over progressively wider windows, and each time arrived at the same leading explanation — a code release pushed minutes before the trouble started. On each pass the proposed explanation came with no safe, reversible action attached, so the automation declined to change anything in production, and it checked the feature-flag history three times, finding no recent flag changes. No action of any kind was taken, and nothing was changed and undone. With the evidence exhausted and no fix identified, the automation handed the incident to a human engineer. The symptoms stopped being reported at the moment of handoff; what ended them is not recorded. Customer impact is described by the error rate and duration reported with the alert, which were measured from the service's own traffic rather than derived here.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only candidate the investigation could support was the deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 2026-09-13T23:59Z — the sole recorded change to io-shop in every lookback window tried, from 24 hours out to six weeks — with latency climbing in the following minute; but the correlation is purely temporal, no rollback or other test was ever run against it, and the logs retrieved were generic latency/timeout lines naming no code path, dependency, flag or resource, so a coincident downstream or resource-exhaustion cause was never ruled out.
